captions.instagram:
How do a kitchen chimney and gas hob work?

A spark of 14,000 volts, a jet of gas that drags in its own air, and a hood that catches smoke it can barely suck. Take an Indian kitchen's gas stove and chimney apart in 3D and see why a good flame is blue.

→ An Indian kitchen: an LPG cylinder, a gas stove, and a chimney above it.
→ Gas flows from the cylinder, through a regulator and hose, to three brass burners.
→ A jet of gas shoots into a tube and drags air in with it, just like a Bunsen burner.
→ Too little air makes a lazy, sooty yellow flame. Enough air and it burns clean and blue.
→ A spark of about 14,000 volts jumps a 4 mm gap and lights the gas.

youtubeLong.title: How do a kitchen chimney and gas hob work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A spark of 14,000 volts, a jet of gas that drags in its own air, and a hood that catches smoke it can barely suck. Take an Indian kitchen's gas stove and chimney apart in 3D and see why a good flame is blue.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/chimneyclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/chimneyclear

In this video:
• Gas from a cylinder, smoke out through a duct. LPG waits as a liquid in a 14.2 kg cylinder at about 5 bar.
• Why a good flame is blue. The gas shoots from a tiny injector into a mixing tube and drags air in with it, the Bunsen principle.
• Thousands of volts to light it, millivolts to keep it safe. The igniter needs about 14,000 volts to make a spark jump a 4 mm gap.
• The chimney doesn't suck the smoke up. At the pan, 70 cm below the hood, a chimney's suction is only about 0.05 m/s.
• Oil can't turn corners. A baffle filter forces the air to zig-zag.
• The number on the box is not the air you get. Rated suction is measured with nothing in the way.
